input.question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?
input.ground_truth: Venus’ day is 243 earth days long. Magellan orbited Venus every 3 hours or so. That means that during a single Venusian day, the probe circled the planet almost 2000 times. I don’t know what you mean by quickly, but it took almost an entire earth year to get that 96%, for what it’s worth.

Question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?

Okay! Imagine you have a big, fluffy pillow and you want to see what’s underneath all the fluff. It’s hard to see just by looking, right? But if you shine a flashlight on it and look at the shadows, you can see the shape of what’s under the pillow!

NASA’s Magellan did something kind of like that, but with Venus, which is a big, cloudy planet covered in thick clouds. Magellan was a special spaceship that sent out invisible radio waves (kind of like shouting with a special voice that can go through clouds). These waves bounced off the surface of Venus and came back to Magellan.

By listening to how the waves bounced back, Magellan could tell if there were mountains, valleys, or flat places on Venus—just like you can tell if something is bumpy or smooth by listening to the sound when you tap it.

Magellan did this all over Venus very quickly, like taking lots of pictures from above without having to land or see through the clouds. That’s how it made a map of Venus fast!
